paragraphs: Paris challenges Menelaus—Helen and Priam look out over the Achaeans from the wall—The covenant is made—Paris and Menelaus fight, and Paris gets the worst of it—Aphrodite carries him off to save him—The scene between him and Helen.

Once the companies were arranged, each under its own captain, the Trojans came on like a flight of wild birds, or of cranes. Cranes scream overhead when rain and winter drive them across the flowing waters of Oceanus to bring death and destruction to the Pygmies, and they squabble in the air as they fly. The Achaeans, by contrast, marched in silence, with high courage and the intention of standing by one another.

It was like the south wind spreading a curtain of mist over the mountain tops, bad for shepherds but better than night for thieves, when a man cannot see farther than he can throw a stone. That was how the dust rose from under their feet as they hurried across the plain.

When the armies were close to one another, Paris came forward as the Trojan champion. He carried a panther’s skin on his shoulders, with his bow and his sword, and he brandished two spears tipped with bronze, challenging the bravest of the Achaeans to meet him in single combat. Menelaus saw him stride out in front of the ranks, and he was glad, like a hungry lion that comes upon the carcass of a goat or a horned stag and devours it on the spot, though dogs and young men attack him. In just that way Menelaus was glad when he caught sight of Paris, because he thought he would now have his revenge. He jumped down from his chariot, in his full suit of armor.

Paris lost his nerve when he saw Menelaus coming toward him. Afraid for his life, he shrank back behind his men. A man who suddenly comes upon a snake in a mountain glade jumps back, trembling and pale. In the same way Paris plunged into the crowd of Trojan warriors, terrified at the sight of the son of Atreus.

Then Hector scolded him. “Paris,” he said, “you evil-hearted Paris, so fair to look at, so mad for women, such a liar. I wish you had never been born, or had died unmarried. That would be better than living to be disgraced and looked at sideways. Will the Achaeans not mock us? They will say we sent a champion who is fair to look at but has no brains and no courage. Is this what you were when you gathered your followers and sailed over the seas? Did you, being what you are, carry off a lovely woman from a far country, married among a people of warriors—bringing sorrow to your father, your city and your whole country, joy to your enemies, and a hang-dog shame to yourself? And now you do not dare face Menelaus and find out what kind of man he is, whose wife you have stolen? Where would your lyre be then, and your love-tricks, your handsome locks and your fair looks, when you were lying in the dust in front of him? The Trojans are a weak-kneed people. Otherwise you would long ago have been given a shirt of stones for the wrongs you have done them.”

And Paris answered, “Hector, you are right to rebuke me. You are as hard as the axe a shipwright swings at his work, cutting the timber to his liking. The edge of your scorn is as keen as that axe in his hand. Still, do not taunt me with the gifts that golden Aphrodite has given me. They are precious. No man should look down on them, since the gods give them where they choose, and nobody can get them by asking. If you want me to fight Menelaus, tell the Trojans and Achaeans to sit down, while he and I fight in the middle for Helen and all her wealth. Whoever wins and proves the better man will take the woman and everything she has and bring them to his home. The rest of you must swear a solemn covenant of peace, by which you Trojans stay here in Troy and the others go home to Argos and the land of the Achaeans.”

Hector was glad to hear this. He went among the Trojan ranks holding his spear by the middle to keep them back, and at his command they all sat down. But the Achaeans kept aiming stones and arrows at him, until Agamemnon shouted to them, “Hold, Argives, do not shoot, sons of the Achaeans. Hector wants to speak.”

They stopped aiming and were still, and Hector spoke. “Trojans and Achaeans,” he said, “hear from my mouth the proposal of Paris, who caused this quarrel. He asks the Trojans and Achaeans to lay their armor on the ground while he and Menelaus fight in the middle for Helen and all her wealth. Whoever wins and proves the better man is to take the woman and everything she has, and bring them to his own home. The rest of us will swear a solemn covenant of peace.”

So he spoke, and they all fell silent, until Menelaus of the loud battle cry addressed them. “Now hear me too,” he said, “for I am the one most wronged. I think the parting of Achaeans and Trojans is near, as it well may be, since so many have suffered for my quarrel with Paris and the wrong he did me. Let whichever of us is to die, die, and let the others fight no more. Bring two lambs, a white ram and a black ewe, for Earth and Sun, and we will bring a third for Zeus. You must also tell Priam to come and swear to the covenant himself. His sons are arrogant and hard to trust, and the oaths of Zeus must not be broken or taken in vain. Young men’s minds are as light as air, but when an old man comes he looks before and after, and considers what will be fairest for both sides.”

The Trojans and Achaeans were glad to hear this, since they thought they would now get some rest. They backed their chariots toward the ranks, climbed out, and took off their armor, laying it on the ground. The two hosts were close together, with only a small space between them. Hector sent two messengers to the city to fetch the lambs and tell Priam to come. Agamemnon told Talthybius to bring the other lamb from the ships, and he did as Agamemnon said.

Meanwhile Iris went to Helen, taking the form of her sister-in-law, the wife of the son of Antenor. Helicaon, son of Antenor, had married Laodice, the fairest of Priam’s daughters. Iris found Helen in her own room, working at a great web of purple linen. On it she was embroidering the battles between Trojans and Achaeans, which Ares had made them fight for her sake. Iris came up close to her and said, “Come here, child, and see the strange things the Trojans and Achaeans are doing. Until now they have been fighting on the plain, mad with the lust of battle. Now they have stopped fighting. They are leaning on their shields and sitting still, with their spears planted beside them. Paris and Menelaus are going to fight over you, and you are to be the wife of the winner.”

So the goddess spoke, and Helen’s heart longed for her former husband, her city and her parents. She threw a white mantle over her head and hurried from her room, weeping as she went. She was not alone. Two of her handmaids went with her, Aethrae, daughter of Pittheus, and Clymene. Soon they were at the Scaean gates.

The two sages Ucalegon and Antenor, elders of the people, were sitting by the Scaean gates with Priam, Panthous, Thymoetes, Lampus, Clytius, and Hiketaon of the race of Ares. They were too old to fight, but they were fluent speakers. They sat on the tower like cicadas that chirp delicately from the branches of some high tree in a wood. When they saw Helen coming toward the tower, they said softly to one another, “No wonder the Trojans and Achaeans have endured so much for so long for the sake of a woman so marvelously and divinely lovely. Still, fair as she is, let them take her and go. Otherwise she will bring sorrow on us and on our children after us.”

But Priam called her to come near. “My child,” he said, “sit in front of me, so you can see your former husband, your kinsmen and your friends. I do not blame you. The gods are to blame, not you. They brought on this terrible war with the Achaeans. Now tell me, who is that huge hero over there, so great and handsome? I have seen men taller by a head, but none so comely and so royal. He must surely be a king.”

“Sir,” Helen answered, “you are my husband’s father, and I hold you dear and honor you. I wish I had chosen death before following your son here, away from my bridal chamber, my friends, my darling daughter and all the companions of my girlhood. It was not to be, and now my life is tears and sorrow. To answer your question: the hero you ask about is Agamemnon son of Atreus, a good king and a brave soldier. As surely as he lives, he is brother-in-law to my hateful and miserable self.”

The old man looked at him in wonder. “Happy son of Atreus,” he said, “child of good fortune. I see that great multitudes of Achaeans are subject to you. Once, in Phrygia, I saw a large force of horsemen, the people of Otreus and of Mygdon, camped on the banks of the river Sangarius. I was their ally, and I was with them when the Amazons, the equals of men, attacked them. Even those were not as many as the Achaeans here.”

Next the old man looked at Odysseus. “Tell me,” he said, “who is that other man, a head shorter than Agamemnon but broader across the chest and shoulders? His armor is laid on the ground, and he strides in front of the ranks like some great woolly ram setting his ewes in order.”
Helen replied, “That man is Odysseus, son of Laertes, a man of great craft. He was born in rugged Ithaca, and no one surpasses him in stratagems and subtle cunning.”

Antenor then said, “Madam, you have spoken truly. Odysseus once came here as an envoy about you, and Menelaus came with him. I received them in my own house, so I know both of them by sight and by conversation. When they stood up before the assembled Trojans, Menelaus had the broader shoulders, but when both were seated Odysseus looked the more royal. After a time they delivered their message. The speech of Menelaus ran trippingly off the tongue. He did not say much, being a man of few words, but he spoke very clearly and to the point, though he was the younger of the two. Odysseus, on the other hand, was silent when he rose to speak, and at first kept his eyes fixed on the ground. He made no play or graceful movement with his scepter. He held it straight and stiff, like a man unpracticed in oratory, and you might have taken him for a mere churl or simpleton. But when he raised his voice and the words came driving from his deep chest like winter snow before the wind, no one could touch him, and nobody thought any more about how he looked.”
Next Priam noticed Ajax. “Who is that huge and handsome warrior?” he asked. “His head and broad shoulders rise above the rest of the Argives.”

“That,” Helen answered, “is huge Ajax, bulwark of the Achaeans. On the other side of him, among the Cretans, stands Idomeneus, looking like a god, with the captains of the Cretans around him. Menelaus often received him as a guest in our house when he came visiting us from Crete. I see many other Achaeans too, whose names I could tell you. But there are two I cannot find anywhere, Castor, breaker of horses, and Pollux the mighty boxer. They are children of my mother, my own brothers. Either they have not left Lacedaemon, or else they have brought their ships but will not show themselves in battle, for the shame and disgrace I have brought on them.”
She did not know that both these heroes were already lying under the earth in their own land of Lacedaemon.

Meanwhile the heralds were carrying the holy oath-offerings through the city: two lambs and a goatskin of wine, the gift of earth. Idaeus carried the mixing-bowl and the golden cups. He came to Priam and said, “Son of Laomedon, the princes of the Trojans and Achaeans call on you to come down to the plain and swear a solemn covenant. Paris and Menelaus are to fight in single combat for Helen, and she and all her wealth will go with whichever of them wins. We are to swear a solemn covenant of peace. Under it the rest of us will live on here in Troy, and the Achaeans will return to Argos and the land of the Achaeans.”

The old man shuddered as he heard this, but he told his followers to yoke the horses, and they did so with all speed. He mounted the chariot and gathered the reins in his hand, and Antenor took his seat beside him. They drove through the Scaean gates onto the plain. When they reached the ranks of the Trojans and Achaeans, they got down from the chariot and walked at a measured pace into the space between the hosts.

Agamemnon and Odysseus both rose to meet them. The attendants brought forward the oath-offerings and mixed the wine in the mixing-bowls. They poured water over the hands of the chieftains. The son of Atreus drew the dagger that hung by his sword and cut wool from the lambs’ heads, and the men-servants handed this around among the Trojan and Achaean princes. Then the son of Atreus lifted up his hands in prayer. “Father Zeus,” he cried, “you who rule from Ida, most glorious in power, and you, Sun, who see and hear all things, Earth and Rivers, and you who in the realms below punish the soul of anyone who has broken his oath, witness these rites and guard them, so that they are not in vain. If Paris kills Menelaus, let him keep Helen and all her wealth, and we will sail home with our ships. But if Menelaus kills Paris, let the Trojans give back Helen and all she has. Let them also pay the Achaeans whatever fine is agreed upon, as a witness among those who will be born hereafter. And if Priam and his sons refuse to pay that fine after Paris has fallen, then I will stay here and go on fighting until I have satisfaction.”

As he spoke he drew his knife across the throats of the victims and laid them on the ground, gasping and dying, for the knife had taken their strength. Then they poured wine from the mixing-bowl into the cups and prayed to the everlasting gods. This was the prayer, Trojans and Achaeans saying it among one another: “Zeus, most great and glorious, and you other everlasting gods, grant that the brains of those who first sin against their oaths—theirs and their children’s—be spilled on the ground just like this wine, and let their wives become the slaves of strangers.”

So they prayed, but Zeus would not yet grant their prayer. Then Priam, descendant of Dardanus, spoke. “Hear me, Trojans and Achaeans,” he said. “I am going back to the wind-beaten city of Ilium. I dare not watch with my own eyes this fight between my son and Menelaus, for only Zeus and the other immortals know which of them will fall.”

With that he laid the two lambs in his chariot and took his seat. He gathered the reins in his hand, Antenor sat beside him, and the two went back to Ilium. Hector and Odysseus measured out the ground. Then they cast lots from a bronze helmet to see which should take aim first. Meanwhile the two hosts lifted their hands and prayed, “Father Zeus, you who rule from Ida, most glorious in power, grant that the man who first brought about this war between us may die and enter the house of Hades, while the rest of us stay at peace and keep our oaths.”

Great Hector turned his head aside as he shook the helmet, and the lot of Paris flew out first. The others took their several stations, each beside his horses and the place where his arms lay. Meanwhile Paris, husband of lovely Helen, put on his fine armor. First he fastened greaves of good make on his legs, fitted with silver ankle-clasps. After that he put on the cuirass of his brother Lycaon and fitted it to his own body. He hung his silver-studded bronze sword about his shoulders, and then his mighty shield. On his handsome head he set a well-made helmet with a horse-hair crest that nodded menacingly above it, and he took up a formidable spear that suited his hands. Menelaus put on his armor in the same way.

When they had armed, each among his own people, they strode into the open space with fierce looks, and Trojans and Achaeans alike were struck with awe at the sight. They stood near each other on the measured ground, brandishing their spears, each furious with the other. Paris aimed first and struck the round shield of the son of Atreus, but the spear did not pierce it, because the shield turned its point. Menelaus took aim next, praying to Father Zeus as he did so. “King Zeus,” he said, “grant me revenge on Paris, who has wronged me. Subdue him under my hand, so that in ages to come men will shrink from doing evil in the house of their host.”

He poised his spear as he spoke and hurled it at the shield of Paris. It went through the shield and the cuirass, and tore the shirt by his flank, but Paris swerved aside and so saved his life. Then the son of Atreus drew his sword and struck at the projecting part of his helmet. The sword shattered into three or four pieces and fell from his hand. Looking up toward Heaven, he cried, “Father Zeus, of all the gods you are the most spiteful. I was sure of my revenge, but now the sword has broken in my hand, my spear was thrown in vain, and I have not killed him.”

With this he flew at Paris, caught him by the horse-hair plume of his helmet, and began dragging him toward the Achaeans. The strap of the helmet under his chin was choking him, and Menelaus would have dragged him off to his own great glory. But Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite was quick to notice and broke the ox-hide strap, so the empty helmet came away in Menelaus’s hand. He flung it to his comrades among the Achaeans and sprang at Paris again to run him through with a spear. But Aphrodite snatched Paris up in a moment (as a god can do), hid him in a cloud of darkness, and carried him to his own bedchamber.

Then she went to fetch Helen, and found her on a high tower, with the Trojan women crowding around her. The goddess took the shape of an old woman who had dressed wool for Helen back in Lacedaemon, and whom Helen loved dearly. Disguised like this, she tugged at Helen’s perfumed robe. “Come with me,” she said. “Paris wants you at the house. He is lying on his bed in his own room, radiant with beauty and dressed in gorgeous clothes. You would never think he had just come from fighting. You would think he was off to a dance, or had just stopped dancing and sat down.”

With these words she stirred Helen’s heart to anger. Helen noticed the goddess’s beautiful neck, her lovely bosom and her sparkling eyes, and she was amazed and said, “Goddess, why do you try to beguile me like this? Are you going to send me still farther afield, to some man you have taken up in Phrygia or fair Meonia? Menelaus has just defeated Paris and is going to take my hateful self back with him. You have come here to betray me. Go and sit with Paris yourself. Give up being a goddess, never let your feet carry you back to Olympus, worry about him and look after him until he makes you his wife—or, for that matter, his slave. But me? I will not go. I can make ready his bed no longer. I would be a by-word among all the women of Troy. Besides, I have trouble on my mind.”

Aphrodite was furious. “Bold hussy,” she said, “do not provoke me. If you do, I will abandon you to your fate and hate you as much as I have loved you. I will stir up fierce hatred between Trojans and Achaeans, and you will come to a bad end.”
Helen was frightened at this. She wrapped her mantle around her and followed the goddess in silence, unnoticed by the Trojan women.

When they reached the house of Paris, the maid-servants went about their work. Helen went into her own room, and the laughter-loving goddess picked up a seat and placed it for her, facing Paris. Helen, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, sat down on it, and with a sidelong look she began to scold her husband.

“So you have come back from the fight,” she said. “I wish you had fallen there instead, by the hand of that brave man who was my husband. You used to brag that you were a better man than Menelaus with hands and spear. Go, then, and challenge him again. But I advise you not to, because if you are foolish enough to meet him in single combat, you will soon fall to his spear.”

And Paris answered, “Wife, do not hurt me with your reproaches. This time Menelaus has beaten me with the help of Athena. Another time I may win, for I too have gods on my side. Come, let us lie down together and make friends. I have never been so passionately in love with you as I am at this moment—not even when I first carried you off from Lacedaemon and sailed away with you, not even when I was with you on the couch of love on the island of Cranae was I so overcome with desire for you as I am now.” With that he led her toward the bed, and his wife went with him.

So they laid themselves down on the bed together. Meanwhile the son of Atreus strode through the crowd, looking everywhere for Paris, and no one, Trojan or ally, could find him. They would not have hidden him if they had seen him, for they all hated him like death itself. Then Agamemnon, king of men, spoke. “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies. The victory has gone to Menelaus. Therefore give back Helen with all her wealth, and pay whatever fine is agreed upon, as a witness among those who will be born hereafter.”
So spoke the son of Atreus, and the Achaeans shouted their approval.
